Use the geometric-series factorization as the main mechanism.

First establish that every root of \(X^p-1\) is a power of the primitive root \(\zeta\): the \(p\) powers of \(\zeta\) are distinct roots, and over a domain a degree-\(p\) polynomial has at most \(p\) roots. Thus \(\eta_1=\zeta^r\) and \(\eta_2=\zeta^s\). Since
\[
\zeta-1\mid \zeta^m-1
\]
for every \(m\), it divides \(\eta_1-\eta_2\).

For the left side of the `Iff`, factor
\[
\zeta^{i+j}-\zeta^i=\zeta^i(\zeta^j-1).
\]
The factor \(\zeta^i\) is a unit. Coprimality of \(j\) and \(n\) provides \(r\) with \(jr\equiv1\pmod n\); geometric-series divisibility then works in both directions between \(\zeta^j-1\) and \(\zeta-1\), proving they are associated.

Prove the right side independently by induction on \(k\), using the standard GCD-monoid inequality
\[
\gcd(a,bc)\mid \gcd(a,b)\gcd(a,c).
\]
The base case follows because \(\gcd(a,1)\) is a unit, and the induction step applies the inequality to \(b^{k+1}=b^k b\). Since both universal assertions in the `Iff` are therefore true, assemble the equivalence by proving each direction without needing its hypothesis.
